newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-WARBURG PROBED ON 300 MILLION STG EUROPEAN SHARE SALE

Investment bank SBC Warburg WSG.L is being investigated by the UK securities industry watchdog over the apparent mishandling of the sale of 300 million stg of European shares for an investment trust. The inquiry, by the Securities and Futures Authority, follows a probe by Warburg's own compliance officials which resulted in two resignations and disciplinary action being taken against several other executives at the bank. The deal resulted in a multi-million pound loss for SBC Warburg.
-SHELL LAUNCHES SMART-CARD REVOLUTION

Anglo-Dutch oil company Shell has announced that a consortium of retailers is to join its customer loyalty scheme, heralding a breakthrough in the use of customer smart cards. Shell will launch its Smart scheme in Scotland on Friday, and in the rest of the UK in the autumn. It will link high street retailers including Dixons, Currys, Victoria Wine, Vision Express and John Menzies with Commercial Union , the RAC and Hilton Hotels. The discount scheme, based on microchip smart cards, is forecast to offer annual average savings of about 50-70 pounds stg to customers.
- EUROPEAN COURT REVERSAL WORRIES CONTRACT WINNERS

A ruling from the European Court of Justice has raised the prospect of contractors facing huge bills for inherited employment liabilities. The ruling, which also threatens the UK government's competitive tendering programme, states that the 1977 European Acquired Rights Directive does not automatically apply when a contracted-out service transfers from one provider to another. This means that in a competitive tender situation, the winning company is not necessarily obliged to take on the staff of the loser, leaving the losing company to meet all staff severance and other liabilities.
- BOEING KEEN FOR NEW JOINT VENTURES WITH BAe

Boeing, the US aircraft manufacturer, has said it would like to increase its ties with British Aerospace (BAe) as part of a campaign to rid itself of its image as an American group. Philip Condit, chairman of Boeing, said that he saw BAe as a possible partner on the planned Joint Strike Fighter, a project for which BAe tendered last year as part of an unsuccessful consortium involving McDonnell Douglas and Northop Grumman of the US. According to Condit, BAe now has the choice of joining either Boeing or Lockheed Martin, the two companies shortlisted by the US government to make the aircraft.
- EU CHIP DECISION PUZZLES INDUSTRY

European manufacturers of personal computers and telecoms equipment have expressed concern about the implications of the EU's decision earlier this week to re-introduce minimum prices on imports of computer memory chips from Japanese and South Korean manufacturers. The complex ruling is expected to increase the price of chips, with South Korean and Japanese manufacturers currently taking about 80 per cent of the $6 billion EU market for D-Ram chips.
- REGULATOR REJECTS ELECTRICITY USERS' PRICING SCHEME

Electricity regulator Professor Stephen Littlechild has upheld a decision by the Electricity Pool to reject a pricing scheme which industrial consumers said would help cut electricity prices. The decision to reject proposals for a 'load management agency' - which would have involved consumers in price setting - prompted an angry response from the Energy Intensive Users Group, the body representing consumers of large amounts of electricity.
- CENTRICA CRITICISED OVER DATABASE MAILSHOT

Centrica, the demerged domestic supply business of British Gas GAS.L, has been criticised by data protection officials over plans to use its database of 19 million customers for a mailshot enquiring whether they wanted to be sent information about extra services. British Gas Trading is to be informed by officials from the Data Protection Registrar that a report is being compiled which could lead to legal action to halt the use of the database - one of the largest in Europe - to market additional services.
- DISCLOSURES IN US ANGER BT INVESTORS

British Telecom is facing the wrath of some of its largest shareholders after the company circulated data about its proposed merger with MCI one month after the US company made the information available in America. MCI disclosed the data in a filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission in February, but BT has only just begun to circulate the information to shareholders in the UK. A company spokesman for BT denied that anybody had been deliberately misinformed or not informed.
- SCOTIA SHARES FALL AS CSM REJECTS DRUG

UK biotechnolgy company Scotia Pharmaceuticals saw its share price slump 24 per cent on Tuesday after the company revealed that the drug Tarabetic, one of its most promising developments, would not earn a recommendation for approval from the UK Committee on the Safety of Medicines. The CSM ruling on Tarabetic, a treatment for the nerve damage suffered by diabetics, follows variations in the apparent performance of the drug in different trial centres. Scotia said it intends to appeal to the medicines commission over the ruling.
- MANAGEMENT AT THOMSON REORGANISED

The French government has pushed through a reorganization of management at the state-controlled Thomson group in preparation for the sell-off of its Thomson Multimedia arm and of the Thomson-CSF defence company. Thierry Breton, who as senior managing director of Bull oversaw the turnaround and privatisation of the computer group, has been appointed chairman of the holding group Thomson SA and of Multimedia, the fully- owned consumer electronics subsidiary. The French government is using the example of Bull - now a going concern in which both NEC and Motorola have large minority stakes - as a template for the privatisation of Multimedia.
